summary: For ages 5–7, teach the butterfly life cycle (egg → caterpillar/larva → chrysalis/pupa → butterfly) as the STAGES OF ONE CREATURE changing, not four different animals. Centre the work on (1) ordering the four stages as a repeating cycle and (2) grasping that the caterpillar and butterfly are the same individual transforming, with the chrysalis as where the body is rebuilt. First-hand observation of a real class caterpillar culture over weeks anchors change-over-time; sequence/animation and labelled-diagram activities reinforce order, vocabulary and the same-creature idea.
misconceptions: 'The caterpillar and butterfly are different animals' — the central misconception; they are one creature at different stages.
'The stages can happen in any order' — the sequence is fixed.
'The chrysalis is asleep/an egg' — not understanding it is the transforming pupa stage.
'It's a straight line that ends at butterfly' — missing that the cycle repeats.
'All baby animals look like small adults' — overgeneralising; metamorphosis is different from simple growth.

activities.title: Observe a real class caterpillar culture over weeks
steps: Keep a class caterpillar culture and look at it regularly over several weeks.
Track and name ONE individual caterpillar, recording what it looks like each day with a drawing or photo.
Draw arrows connecting your day-by-day pictures to show it is one creature's story moving through caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly (starting from the egg only if your culture began with eggs).
After the butterfly emerges, say aloud whether it is the same creature you have been watching and how you know.
activities.insight: The caterpillar and the butterfly are the SAME individual changing over time; the stages happen in a fixed order and take real time.

activities.title: Order the four stages into a repeating ring
steps: Take four shuffled picture cards — a tiny egg, a fat caterpillar, a chrysalis, a butterfly.
Arrange them into a RING rather than a straight line, so the cycle can start again.
Place a card showing the butterfly laying eggs on a leaf to close the loop back to the egg.
Say out loud why it is a cycle that repeats and not a line that ends at the butterfly.
activities.insight: The life cycle has a fixed order AND it repeats — the butterfly lays eggs that hatch into new caterpillars, so the cycle begins again with the next generation (the butterfly itself does not turn back into an egg).

activities.title: Label the cycle and learn both names for each stage
steps: Work with a circular four-stage diagram and reveal a short fact about each stage (egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly).
For each stage, match the familiar name to the technical name: caterpillar = larva, chrysalis = pupa.
Say what is happening at each stage, including that inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is being rebuilt (not sleeping).
activities.insight: Each stage has a name and a role; the technical terms larva and pupa name the caterpillar and chrysalis stages, and the chrysalis is where the body transforms.

activities.title: Retell or draw the transformation
steps: After reading a story (e.g. The Very Hungry Caterpillar, which calls the chrysalis a 'cocoon' — real butterflies form a chrysalis, while moths spin cocoons) or watching the real change happen, retell the transformation from caterpillar to butterfly.
Draw the sequence, showing the same creature at each stage.
Answer: is the butterfly the same creature that was the caterpillar, or a new one, and how do you know?
activities.insight: Children can reconstruct the ordered transformation themselves and explain it as one creature changing.

activities.title: Compare different kinds of change (extension)
steps: Consider a grasshopper, which hatches as a nymph that looks like a small grasshopper without working wings, and grows bigger by shedding its skin several times, with its wings developing gradually and no chrysalis.
Consider a tadpole that turns into a frog.
For each, say whether the change is more like the caterpillar's story (a big body rebuild) or more like simple growing bigger, and why.
activities.insight: A dramatic whole-body change (like caterpillar to butterfly, or tadpole to frog) is different from mostly growing bigger, where the young already looks much like a small adult (like a grasshopper nymph, which has no chrysalis); this distinguishes real understanding from memorised stages.

checkQuestion: A child says: 'The caterpillar and the butterfly are two different animals — the caterpillar dies inside the chrysalis and a brand-new butterfly comes out.' Is that right? Tell me what really happens, and why.
checkAnswer: It is not right — the caterpillar does NOT die. It is the SAME animal changing its body. Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body is rebuilt (reorganised) into a butterfly. So one creature goes through stages: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly. It transforms; it is not replaced by a new animal.
